title: Staying Safe · Episode 4
chapters: Lost in the bush: how to be found

units.t: Staying Safe. Episode four.
In this episode: Staying alive on long drives, Reading a map and compass and Lost in the bush: how to be found.
Part one. Staying alive on long drives.
Australia's long, empty roads are beautiful, but fatigue, wildlife and remote breakdowns catch out even experienced drivers.
Here is how to make every road trip end safely.
The hypnotic road.
There is something hypnotic about a long Australian highway: straight bitumen, red dirt, a horizon that never gets closer.
That is part of the danger.
Most Australians live in cities, yet a large share of road deaths happen on rural and regional roads, often in single-vehicle crashes where a car leaves the road or hits a tree.
Speeds are higher, roads may be narrow or unsealed, and help can be hours away.
Road safety campaigns talk about the 'fatal five': speeding, drink and drug driving, not wearing a seatbelt, fatigue and distraction.
On long drives the last two matter most, because they creep up on people who felt fine when they set out.
Fatigue and microsleeps.
Being awake for a long time impairs reactions and judgement in a way research has compared to having alcohol in your blood.
The scariest part is the microsleep: a few seconds when your brain switches off, often without you realising.
At 100 kilometres per hour a car covers nearly 28 metres every second, so a four-second microsleep carries you well over 100 metres with nobody in control.
Warning signs include yawning, heavy eyes, drifting in your lane, missing signs and not remembering the last few kilometres.
Opening the window or turning up the music does not fix tiredness.
The only real cure is sleep, so pull over somewhere safe for a rest or a power nap.
Planning to beat fatigue.
Fatigue is far easier to prevent than to fight.
Start a long drive well rested, and avoid setting out after a full day of work or when your body normally sleeps, such as late at night and in the mid-afternoon slump.
Road safety agencies commonly recommend a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours.
Get out, walk around, and have a drink and a snack.
Look for Driver Reviver sites, which often operate on major highways in holiday periods and offer free tea, coffee and a chat.
If you can, share the driving with another licensed driver.
Be honest about how far you can go.
An extra night in a motel is a small price compared with the cost of a crash.
Animals, trains and gravel.
Kangaroos, wallabies, wombats, emus and livestock are a real hazard, especially at dawn, dusk and night.
Slow down where wildlife signs appear and scan the verges for eyes reflecting your headlights.
If an animal jumps out, brake firmly in a straight line.
Many serious crashes happen when drivers swerve, lose control and hit a tree or oncoming vehicle.
Kangaroos can change direction suddenly, and where there is one there are often more.
Road trains, trucks towing several trailers, can stretch beyond 50 metres.
Pass only with a long, clear view ahead.
If one approaches on a narrow road, slow down and move left.
On gravel, drive slower, avoid harsh braking and steering, and keep your headlights on in dust.
Check road conditions first, as roads may close after rain.
Remote breakdowns and help.
Before heading remote, tell someone your route and arrival time.
Carry far more water than you think you need, plus food, a first aid kit, a spare tyre and tools.
Mobile coverage vanishes across much of Australia, so many travellers carry a satellite device or personal locator beacon.
If you break down, stay with your vehicle.
It is far easier for searchers to spot than a person, and it gives shade.
People have died walking away in extreme heat.
After a crash, get clear of traffic and turn on your hazard lights.
Call Triple Zero, 000, if someone is hurt or trapped, a vehicle is on fire or the road is blocked.
The free Emergency+ app shows your GPS location to read to the operator.
A first aid course will prepare you to help.
The key idea: Country roads carry a disproportionate share of Australia's road deaths, and fatigue and distraction are the quiet killers on long drives.
Part two. Reading a map and compass.
Phones die, satellites drop out and screens are hard to read in the rain.
A paper map and a compass need no battery, and the skills to use them are surprisingly learnable.
Paper and scale.
Phone navigation is brilliant until the battery goes flat in the cold, the screen cracks or you lose signal in a deep valley.
Bushwalking clubs and search and rescue groups in Australia still advise carrying a paper map and compass, and knowing how to use them, as a backup.
Navigating with a map also makes you read the land and notice ridges and creeks.
People following a blue dot often have little idea of their surroundings.
Walking maps are usually topographic, with scales such as 1:25,000 or 1:50,000.
On a 1:25,000 map, one centimetre is 250 metres; on a 1:50,000 map, 500 metres.
The larger the second number, the more ground the map covers and the less detail.
Map distance is flat, so a steep kilometre takes longer than a level one.
Contours and grid references.
Each contour line joins points of the same height, and the contour interval is in the legend.
Close lines mean steep ground; wide spacing means gentle ground.
Stacked closed rings mark a hill or peak.
V or U shapes pointing uphill show a valley or gully, often with a creek.
Pointing downhill, they show a spur, a ridge running down from higher ground.
A grid reference describes a location precisely, perhaps to rescuers.
Australian topographic maps use the Map Grid of Australia, with vertical lines called eastings and horizontal lines called northings.
Give the easting first, then the northing: ‘along the corridor, then up the stairs’.
A four-figure reference identifies a grid square, usually one kilometre across.
Six figures estimate tenths within it, to about 100 metres.
Norths and bearings.
True north is the geographic North Pole.
Grid north follows the map's vertical grid lines and is very close to true north.
Magnetic north is where your compass points.
The difference is magnetic declination.
In Australia it ranges from near zero in parts of Western Australia to over ten degrees east in the south-east.
Maps print the declination.
A ten-degree error over five kilometres puts you almost a kilometre off course.
To take a bearing, lay a baseplate compass's edge on the map joining where you are to where you are going, with its arrow pointing to the destination.
Turn the dial until the orienting lines parallel the grid lines, with the orienting arrow to the top of the map.
Read the bearing, then correct for declination: where it is east, subtract it.
Walking on a bearing.
Hold the compass flat with the direction-of-travel arrow pointing ahead.
Turn your whole body until the red, north end of the needle sits inside the orienting arrow, often remembered as ‘red in the shed’.
The arrow now points along your bearing.
Rather than staring at the compass, pick a distinct landmark in that direction, walk to it, then repeat.
Keep the compass away from metal, phones, car bodies and power lines, which can pull the needle.
Another technique is aiming off: when heading for a point on a creek or track, deliberately aim to one side so you know which way to turn on arrival.
A compass for here.
Earth's magnetic field also dips downward at an angle that changes with latitude.
A compass needle is weighted to cancel that dip in the region where it will be used.
A compass balanced for Europe or North America may tilt, drag on its housing and read sluggishly in Australia.
Check it is balanced for the southern hemisphere or Australian zone, or choose a global needle.
Practise somewhere safe and familiar, such as a local park or well-marked track, before relying on your skills in remote country.
And always tell someone your plans and carry an emergency beacon where there is no phone coverage.
The key idea: A paper map and compass never run out of battery, and a map's scale tells you real distances.
Part three. Lost in the bush: how to be found.
Every year in Australia, bushwalkers, campers and tourists get lost, and most are found alive.
The ones who do best usually prepared before they left and stayed calm once things went wrong.
How people get lost.
Few people set out for an adventure that ends in a police search.
More often it starts small.
A walker follows a faint side trail that looks like a shortcut.
A day hike runs late and the light fades.
Mist rolls over a ridge and every gum tree looks the same.
A tired walker takes a wrong turn at an unmarked junction and keeps going, hoping the track will reconnect.
Search and rescue teams know these patterns well.
People rarely realise they are lost straight away, and the urge to keep moving and fix the problem quickly often carries them further from where searchers will look.
Plan and beacon.
The most important safety step happens before you leave home.
Tell a reliable person your route, when you expect to be back and when to raise the alarm.
Check the weather, fire danger ratings and park alerts.
Carry extra water and food, warm and waterproof layers, a torch, a first aid kit, and a map and compass or GPS, and know how to use them.
Do not rely on a phone alone, since coverage is patchy and batteries die.
A personal locator beacon sends a distress signal by satellite to the Australian Maritime Safety Authority.
Most include GPS, work almost anywhere with a clear view of the sky and need no subscription.
Register yours with AMSA for free, and only activate it in a genuine life-threatening emergency.
Stop and think.
The moment you realise you do not know where you are, the most useful thing you can do is stop.
Many outdoor organisations teach STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan.
Sit down, have a drink of water and let the first rush of panic pass.
Think about when you last knew for certain where you were.
Observe the time of day, the weather and how much water, food and battery you have.
Then plan.
If you can confidently retrace your steps to a known point, that may be sensible.
If not, the best plan is usually to stay where you are, especially if someone knows your trip plan.
Wandering further makes you harder to find, burns energy and water, and can lead into steep or dangerous country.
Shelter, water, warmth.
Survival instructors use a rough rule of threes: around three hours in harsh conditions without shelter, around three days without water and around three weeks without food.
The numbers vary greatly, but the order is useful.
In hot conditions, find shade, rest through the heat of the day and ration your effort rather than your water, drinking what you need.
In cold, wet or windy conditions, which occur in alpine areas and Tasmania even in summer, hypothermia is a serious danger.
Put on all your layers, get out of the wind, and insulate yourself from the cold ground with leaves, a pack or anything dry.
Food matters least.
Most people can go several days without eating and still be found in reasonable health.
Helping searchers find you.
Move to a clearing, track or open ridge if it is safe, as thick canopy hides you from the air.
Lay out bright clothing or a space blanket.
Three of anything, such as three whistle blasts, three flashes of light or three piles of rocks, is widely recognised as a distress signal.
A whistle carries much further than a voice and uses less energy.
A small mirror or phone screen can flash sunlight at aircraft.
If you have reception, call Triple Zero, 000, and ask for police, who coordinate land searches.
Your call can connect through another carrier's network, and the Emergency+ app shows your GPS coordinates.
Then stay put, follow instructions and keep your phone in low power mode.
A text to family may get through when a call will not.
The key idea: Getting lost usually starts with small, ordinary mistakes, and the urge to keep moving often makes it worse.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why are long country drives especially risky?
Answer. Higher speeds, fatigue and help being far away.
Question two. On a 1:50,000 map, what does one centimetre represent?
Answer. 500 metres.
Question three. What often carries lost walkers further from where searchers will look?
Answer. The urge to keep moving to fix things fast.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
